topic: Is a domain reset a global budget reset, and does that matter?
provenance: Open lead left by a reviewer terminated mid-run by a usage limit. Recorded as an open question, then investigated by the author. NOT a reviewer finding - that review produced no verdict.
mechanism: A window_seconds change is a new epoch domain, which re-seeds the key. Every bucket_key is derived from the epoch key, so all bucket keys change and every client effectively starts a fresh bucket.

isItAttackerReachable.evidence: Measured has_table_privilege for service_role, anon and authenticated across limiter.config, key_state, bucket, grant and translation_prefix, for SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Not one privilege is held. The schema grants only USAGE plus EXECUTE on the three clockless entry points.
isItAttackerReachable.consequence: Triggering a domain reset requires direct database or owner access. It is an operator action, not something the app role or a guest can reach.

canThePeriodicReseedResetBudgetsMidWindo.reasoning: A reseed_interval re-seed only occurs inside the ratchet loop while ADVANCING the epoch. Advancing the epoch also changes window_id, so the bucket is new regardless. A same-window re-seed is not reachable through that path.

residualTradeoff.statement: An operator who changes window_seconds mid-window resets every guest's budget once.
residualTradeoff.severity: Operator footgun, not a security defect. It grants a one-time fresh budget to everyone, including any abuser active at that moment.
residualTradeoff.alternativeConsidered: Preserving the old epoch across a domain change is exactly the r3 wedge: the epoch pins at an unreachable value and guest reporting is denied permanently with no self-healing path.
residualTradeoff.chosen: A bounded one-time reset is strictly preferable to permanent denial of service, particularly for an accessibility app where refusing a legitimate reporter is the worse failure.
residualTradeoff.recommendation: window_seconds should be treated as a rare, deliberate operational change, not a routine tuning knob. Production thresholds remain DEFERRED, so no value is being fixed here.

notAVerdict: This analysis does not substitute for the fourth independent review, which must still run against the unchanged artifact.

AUTHOR_CORRECTION_AFTER_R4_REVIEW.whatIGotWrong: This file concluded the domain reset was a "bounded, one-time operator footgun". It was NEITHER bounded NOR one-time, and the r4 reviewer proved both.
AUTHOR_CORRECTION_AFTER_R4_REVIEW.defect1: Revisiting a previously-used window_seconds re-seeded AGAIN each time. Reproduced by the author: one source obtained 7 distinct bucket keys and 8 units against an allowance of 2.
AUTHOR_CORRECTION_AFTER_R4_REVIEW.defect2: RAISING window_seconds stranded every existing row permanently, because purge() computes its cutoff in the new, numerically smaller epoch numbering and can never reach the older larger window_ids. Reproduced: cutoff 20706 vs a stranded window_id of 29817134.
AUTHOR_CORRECTION_AFTER_R4_REVIEW.whyMyAnalysisMissedIt: I examined only a single change in one direction. I did not examine revisits, and I did not examine the interaction with purge cutoffs across domains.
AUTHOR_CORRECTION_AFTER_R4_REVIEW.resolution: Superseded by the structural fix in v4-r5: limiter.guard_window_domain refuses a window_seconds change while limiter.bucket has rows, so neither defect is reachable.
AUTHOR_CORRECTION_AFTER_R4_REVIEW.twoClaimsThatDIDHold: Independently confirmed by the reviewer: no role holds any privilege on any limiter table, and the periodic reseed cannot reset budgets mid-window.
